cards.title: Sliding window
cards.evidence: Cold revisits 64% (11). Minimum Window Substring failed 4 of 6 cold revisits.
cards.hook: A caterpillar: the head (r) always moves forward; the tail (l) moves forward only to restore a broken rule.
triggers: longest / shortest / count with a condition
"at most k distinct", "contains all of t"
invariant: After the inner while-loop, the window [l, r] is VALID; every r is the right end exactly once.
Works only when validity is monotone: shrinking a valid window never makes it invalid (for "at most" rules), or growing never fixes it (for "shortest cover").
cards.five_min: contiguous + monotone condition → window. Longest-valid: expand r, shrink while invalid, record after. Shortest-cover: expand r, while valid record then shrink. O(n), map of counts.
explain: Two shapes. LONGEST valid window: add s[r]; while the window breaks the rule, remove s[l++]; now record r-l+1. SHORTEST window that covers: add s[r]; while it still covers, record and remove s[l++].
Count of subarrays with "exactly k" is not monotone. Compute atMost(k) − atMost(k−1); in atMost, each r adds (r − l + 1) subarrays ending at r.

For Minimum Window Substring keep need[c] and one integer "missing" = characters still needed. Adding c: if need[c]-- > 0 then missing--. Removing c: if ++need[c] > 0 then missing++. Your TLE came from re-checking the whole map on every step (O(52) per move on 10⁵ chars, plus a map copy).

cards.title: Prefix sums + hashing
cards.evidence: Only 4 problems; cold 62% (8). Never accepted: Range Sum Query 2D, Max Sum of 3 Non-Overlapping Subarrays. Continuous Subarray Sum failed 2 of 2 cold.

count of pairs with a property of P[j] − P[i]
invariant: sum(i..j) = P[j+1] − P[i] with P[0] = 0.
Scan j left to right; the map holds every earlier prefix (value → count or first index). Put P[0] = 0 in the map before the loop.
cards.five_min: "subarray with sum/property" + negatives → prefix + hash map of earlier prefixes; answer += count[P − k]. Range queries → prefix array (2D: inclusion–exclusion). Range updates → difference array.
explain: Count subarrays with sum k: at each j you ask "how many earlier prefixes equal P − k?" A hash map answers that in O(1). The seed map[0] = 1 counts subarrays starting at index 0 — forgetting it is the classic bug.
Divisible by k: store P mod k (normalise negatives: ((P % k) + k) % k). Two equal remainders → the sum between them is divisible by k. For "length ≥ 2" store the FIRST index of each remainder.
2D: S[i+1][j+1] = a[i][j] + S[i][j+1] + S[i+1][j] − S[i][j]. Query (r1,c1)-(r2,c2) = S[r2+1][c2+1] − S[r1][c2+1] − S[r2+1][c1] + S[r1][c1]. The +1 offset removes all boundary ifs (your [[-1]] bug).

answer range huge (up to 1e9–1e14) but feasibility is O(n)
monotone: if x works, every bigger (or smaller) x works
invariant: feasible(x) is monotone. lo = smallest possible answer, hi = a value KNOWN to be feasible.

cards.title: Monotonic stack and deque

cards.hook: A queue at a ticket counter where a taller person arriving makes everyone shorter behind them leave: they will never be "the tallest" again.
triggers: sum over all subarrays of min/max (contribution)
invariant: Stack holds indices whose values are monotone (e.g. decreasing for "next greater"). When x pops an index, x is that index's answer.
Each index is pushed and popped once → O(n).
Contribution: a[i] is the min of (i − prevLess) × (nextLessOrEqual − i) subarrays; use strict on one side, non-strict on the other to count ties once.
cards.five_min: Ask "who is the first element to my right/left that beats me?" → monotonic stack. "Sum over all subarrays of min" → contribution with prev/next smaller. "Max in every window" → deque with front expiry.

Ties: with [2,2], both 2s would claim [2,2] if both sides were strict. Use "previous strictly less" and "next less or equal" so exactly one of them claims it.

cards.title: Trie
cards.evidence: Cold 0 of 4 (Word Search II). Same word reported twice; "oa" missed when it was a prefix of "oaa"; TLE on a 12×12 board.
cards.hook: A tree of letters where each path from the root spells a prefix; a flag (or the word itself) marks where a word ends.
triggers: search a board or stream for many words at once
invariant: Node = 26 children + word marker. A word ends at a node; prefixes continue below it, so finding a word does NOT stop the DFS.
In Word Search II store the word at its end node and clear it when found (no duplicates); prune empty leaves to stay fast.
cards.five_min: Many patterns against one text/board → build a trie of the patterns, walk text/board once. Single word → plain DFS. O(cells · 4 · 3^(L−1)) worst, pruning helps.
explain: Why your Word Search II reported "oa" twice: the same word can be reached by two different board paths. Storing the word at the end node and setting it to "" after the first hit fixes it.
Why "oa" was missed when "oaa" existed: you stopped the DFS (or returned) when you found a word. A word end is not a leaf; keep going into the children.

Speed: walk the trie node together with the board cell (pass the child pointer), mark the cell visited by overwriting it with "#", restore it on return, and delete a child when it has no words below it.

cards.title: The DP ladder: recursion → memo → table → space
cards.evidence: Your strongest habit: Stocks IV shows the full ladder with reasons. DP grid/strings failures were base cases, not state design.
cards.hook: Write the brute-force recursion that tries every choice. If the same arguments repeat, cache them. If you know the order, fill a table. If a row only needs the previous row, keep two rows.
triggers: count ways / min cost / max value / can we reach
choices at each step, and subproblems overlap
constraints around 10³–10⁴ for O(n²), or two indices
invariant: State = the smallest set of arguments that fully describes "what is left to decide".
Transition = try every choice from this state; answer = best/sum over choices.
Every return in the memo function goes through memo[...] =.
cards.five_min: 1 Say the recursion in words: f(i, …) = answer for the suffix/prefix starting at i given … . 2 Choices and the transition. 3 Base cases (empty, 1 element). 4 State count × transition cost = complexity. 5 Decide: memo (fast to write) or table (order is clear, space can shrink).
explain: How to find the state: write the brute force with the arguments that change between calls. Drop any argument that can be derived from the others. What remains is the state. E.g. House Robber: rob(i) = max(rob(i+1), a[i] + rob(i+2)) → state is just i.

How to convert memo → table: the table index order must evaluate every dependency first. If f(i) uses f(i+1), f(i+2), fill i from n−1 down to 0. If dp[i][j] uses dp[i−1][j] and dp[i][j−1], fill rows top to bottom, columns left to right.
Space: if row i only reads row i−1, keep two rows (or one row with the right loop direction: 0/1 knapsack goes right→left so you do not reuse an item).

Identify the DP family fast: 1D linear (house robber, decode), grid (paths), knapsack (pick items with capacity), strings (two indices i, j), LIS (ending at i), interval (l, r: choose a split or the last action), state machine (stocks: holding or not), tree (return a tuple per node), bitmask (set of used items).

cards.title: Fenwick tree and segment tree
cards.evidence: Only 2 problems (Range Module, Count of Pairs), both Hard, no cold data. A typical Big Tech gap.
cards.hook: A prefix-sum array that survives updates. Fenwick: each index stores the sum of a block whose size is its lowest set bit. Segment tree: each node stores the answer for a range, children split it in half.
triggers: count of smaller / greater elements before or after (inversions)
invariant: Fenwick: t[i] covers (i − lowbit(i), i]. Update climbs i += i & −i; query descends i −= i & −i. 1-indexed.
Segment tree: node covers [l, r]; leaf = element; internal = combine(left, right). Query visits O(log n) nodes.
cards.five_min: Sum/count with point updates → Fenwick (10 lines). Min/max, or range updates, or custom combine → segment tree. Values up to 10⁹ → compress to ranks first.
explain: Count of smaller numbers after self: scan from the right; for each x, answer = query(rank(x) − 1) = how many already-inserted values are smaller; then add(rank(x), 1). Compression maps values to 1..m.
Fenwick on [5, 2, 6, 1] scanning right→left: insert 1 → for 6: count ranks < rank(6) = 1; insert 6 → for 2: count < 2 = 1 (the 1); insert 2 → for 5: count < 5 = 2. Answer [2, 1, 1, 0].

Segment tree is worth it when the combine is not invertible (max, gcd) or when you need range updates with lazy propagation. In an interview, the iterative bottom-up segment tree (size 2n) is the shortest to write.

cards.title: String hashing and KMP
cards.evidence: Repeated DNA Sequences seen once; no KMP or rolling-hash problem on your list. A typical Big Tech gap for string rounds.
cards.hook: Turn a substring into a number in O(1) with prefix hashes, so substring equality is a number comparison. KMP: when a match fails, the pattern's own prefix table tells you where to resume.
triggers: substring equality checks, many of them
longest repeated / duplicate substring (binary search + hash)
pattern search in text in O(n + m)
invariant: H[i] = hash of s[0..i); hash(l, r) = H[r] − H[l]·P^(r−l) (mod). Use a 64-bit mod or two mods to avoid collisions.
KMP lps[i] = length of the longest proper prefix of p[0..i] that is also a suffix.
cards.five_min: Many substring comparisons → prefix hashes. "Longest X" over lengths with a monotone property → binary search on length + hash set. Exact single pattern → KMP (or Z-function).

followups.idea: If length L repeats, so does every shorter length (monotone). Binary search L; check with a set of rolling hashes of all length-L windows.

followups.idea: The longest palindromic prefix of s = lps of t = s + "#" + reverse(s) at the last index. Prepend reverse of the remaining suffix.
followups.code_delta: string t = s + "#" + string(s.rbegin(), s.rend()); int k = lps(t).back(); return string(s.rbegin(), s.rend()).substr(0, s.size() - k) + s;
